Designing the WayAuto icon

I designed an app icon for WayAuto, an automatic driving log.

Where it started

The WayAuto team shared two sketches, both with a car at the end of a blue W. One was drawn from above. The other tilted the scene so the road swung back in perspective. What stayed with me was how much that blue line could do. It was the road under the car, the trace of a drive, and the first letter of WayAuto.

WayAuto records drives automatically. As I used it, I kept coming back to the License tab and the idea of having a record of where I’d been. I wanted the icon to capture that feeling. I kept the blue route from the sketches and began drawing the rest of the name into the streets around it.

Drawing WAY as roads

I used aerial photos to study how roads bend, meet, and split. I wanted the streets to feel believable enough that you could see a map at a glance, then find the W, A, and Y when you looked closer.

W · The switchback

The hairpins in the aerial photo have different lengths and radii. I borrowed that uneven rhythm for the W, giving it a slight left lean and letting one bend sit lower than the other. In one version, the final stroke got lost against the blue route. I left a little more space between them so the full W could still read.

A · The traffic island

At the junction, I noticed the triangles of ground between the turning lanes. I used that negative space for the opening in the A and made a connecting lane its crossbar. I shifted and rotated the junction until the triangle held its shape and the road looked like it could continue past the edge of the icon.

Y · The fork

The aerial fork gave me the Y almost as it was. I kept the two sweeping branches and, after feedback on the draft, straightened the stem so it ran cleanly into the bottom edge. I matched the widths of the three letter roads and switched the W and A into reading order. That helped the letters feel like streets drawn on the same map.

Building the icon in Icon Composer

I returned to the overhead sketch and dropped the silver badge so the coupe could sit directly on the road. With the car and the streets in the same perspective, I could give the coupe more room without losing the surrounding letterforms. I laid the silhouette and the road curves against the icon grid to check where they met and where they needed space.

In Icon Composer, I built the icon in four groups. The charcoal map formed the base. The W switchback, A junction, Y fork, and left approach each had their own vector path. I separated the blue route from its glow, then placed the white coupe and its contact shadow at the top.

Working in layers let me adjust a bend without shifting the coupe, or soften the glow while keeping the blue route vivid. I brought the lightest part of the cobalt-to-ice gradient right up to the hood to draw the eye to the car. At home-screen size, I checked that the white silhouette read right away and the charcoal streets still held together around it.

I delivered the editable Icon Composer project, a PNG export, and the individual artwork layers so the WayAuto team could use the icon and keep refining it.

The finished icon

My favorite part is that the simple idea in those first sketches is still there. The white coupe catches my eye, the blue route gives it somewhere to go, and the streets around it quietly spell WAY.
